items.title: Factors Affecting Student Satisfaction and Utilization of the Learning Management System (LMS): A Case Study at the University of Cape Coast.
items.abstract: This study investigates factors affecting students’ satisfaction and utilisation of the Learning Management System (LMS) at the University of Cape Coast (UCC), Ghana, in line with the mandate of the National ICT Policy (2020) to integrate LMS into institutions. Despite LMS platforms being critical to blended learning, student satisfaction remains inconsistent due to infrastructural and pedagogical challenges. The research employs a mixed-methods explanatory sequential design, integrating quantitative analysis of survey data from 635 students and qualitative insights from open-ended responses. Stratified random sampling ensured demographic representation across modes of study (regular, distance, sandwich, and affiliation), level of study, age groups, and gender. The key findings show that technical infrastructure is the primary driver of satisfaction (β = -0.41, p < 0.001), with distance students reporting the most technical issues (40% "Very Often") and the lowest satisfaction levels (3.15). Lecturer interaction emerged as an essential mediator (β = 0.28), helping to reduce technical dissatisfaction, while resource accessibility (β = 0.17) was necessary but insufficient without technical stability. Notable demographic differences were observed: satisfaction increased with age (16–22: 3.12; 51+: 4.35; r = 0.38), and students in the regular mode outperformed those in the distance mode of study (4.28 vs. 3.15; β = 0.22). Thematic analysis identified technical issues (42%), resource gaps (28%), and support services (18%) as key areas for improvement. The study advances the Context-Integrated LMS Satisfaction (C-LMS) model, resolving limitations of existing frameworks (TAM, UTAUT, IQT) by incorporating Ghana-specific barriers (e.g., bandwidth, infrastructure deficits) and demographic moderators. Recommendations include: first, short-term technical triage (offline modules, 24/7 support); second, medium-term infrastructure upgrades (50% bandwidth increase); third, long-term systemic transformation (AI-driven issue prediction, a national LMS consortium). These findings provide a blueprint for enhancing the LMS resilience in resource-constrained contexts, emphasising that technical stability and human factors are interdependent in driving satisfaction.

items.title: Faculty and Student Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education at a Public Sector University in Pakistan: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI), with its range of applications and ease of use, is transforming medicine. AI usage is increasing exponentially in a resource-limited country like Pakistan; however, application in medical education is evolving and needs to be understood. Little work has been done on perceptions among faculty and students to understand their understanding and readiness to use AI, while keeping in mind the ethical issues it may raise. Objective: To explore perceptions of faculty and students regarding integration of AI into undergraduate medical education, potential challenges and ethical considerations in adoption of AI, at a public sector university in Pakistan. Methods: Exploratory descriptive qualitative study at Dow University of Health Sciences, Karachi, from October 2025 to March 2026, including faculty in-depth interviews (IDI) and focus group discussions (FGD) with MBBS students till data saturation was achieved. Audio recording and transcription were done using an artificial intelligence tool. Data were thematically analyzed using the Braun and Clarke framework. Results: A total of 10 IDIs and 5 FGDs were conducted. IDIs included 10 faculty members: 6 (60%) females and 4 (40%) males, aged 38-55 years. FGDs included 40 students (males: 15, females: 25), with 7-8 participants per FGD, aged 20-25 years. Six key themes were derived: Modernization in Education, Curriculum Integration, Clinical Research and Practice, Ethics and Professional Responsibility, Readiness of the Institute, Strategic Integration, and Governance Issues. Conclusion: Faculty and students see AI as a supportive tool that increases access to healthcare and information and reduces errors. Important concerns raised included confidentiality, privacy, and fear of AI replacing humans in the medical sector.

items.title: Field-Wave Algebra (FWA): Mathematical Foundations of Dynamic Systems, Consciousness, and Error Loops
items.abstract: This work introduces Field-Wave Algebra (FWA), a mathematical framework that models reality as a system of dynamic field states, error-driven evolution, and recursive return processes. Instead of treating numbers, matter, consciousness, and information as isolated static entities, FWA describes them as manifestations of continuous field dynamics. The framework is built around the relationship between structural deviation, error magnitude, and return operators, expressed through a fundamental consciousness equation and a hierarchy of evolving system states. The model spans inert matter, biological organisms, artificial intelligence, and large-scale cosmic structures within a unified formalism. A central concept of FWA is the loop structure 0 → S → 0, where systems evolve away from equilibrium and attempt to restore balance through recursive feedback mechanisms. Error is interpreted not as a defect but as a generative force driving adaptation, complexity, and emergent organization. The paper presents mathematical foundations for dynamic state evolution, field correction processes, self-organization, and number resonance. Artificial intelligence is analyzed as an open-loop architecture capable of state generation but lacking autonomous loop closure. Numbers are interpreted as active wave resonances rather than static symbols, leading to a process-oriented view of mathematics. FWA proposes a unified perspective linking consciousness, dynamic systems, information processing, error propagation, and mathematical structure within a single field-based framework.

items.title: From Barriers to Solutions: Exploring Knowledge and Health-Protective Behaviours of Wildland Firefighters in Queensland, Australia
items.abstract: Wildfires are an escalating natural hazard in Australia and a growing public health concern. Exposure to wildfire smoke is associated with acute and chronic adverse health effects, placing wildland firefighters at elevated risk due to recurrent occupational exposure. Although protective behaviours and personal protective equipment (PPE) are recommended, uptake remains inconsistent due to operational and behavioural barriers. This descriptive qualitative study applied the Health Belief Model to explore firefighters’ risk awareness, protective practices, motivators, and barriers. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with eleven wildland firefighters in Southeast Queensland, Australia. Participants demonstrated strong awareness of short-term health effects, informed by personal experience, but limited understanding of long-term health risks. Compliance with mandatory PPE (clothing, gloves, boots, helmets) was high and motivated by prevention of immediate injury. However, respiratory protective equipment use was inconsistent due to discomfort, poor fit, communication difficulties, and operational constraints. Additional barriers to health-protective behaviours included limited decontamination access and inequities in PPE design, particularly for women. Participants identified improved health education, practical PPE options, and further research as priorities for strengthening occupational health protection. Addressing these barriers through improved knowledge translation, organisational support, and approaches such as cultural burning may reduce exposure and improve workforce health.

items.title: From Disciplinary Formation to Artistic Autonomy: Higher Art Education in France and Armenia in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Higher art education is undergoing a significant transformation as traditional models of disciplinary and technical formation increasingly intersect with artistic autonomy, research-oriented practice, interdisciplinary learning, and artificial intelligence (AI). The article examines how educational structures and institutional cultures shape the formation of artists and designers, focusing comparatively on France and Armenia. The relevance of the topic is determined by the need to understand how contemporary institutions organise the transition from disciplinary knowledge toward independent creative agency at a moment when AI is reshaping established understandings of technical skill, authorship, and artistic decision-making. The aim of the study is to determine how different educational cultures shape the development of artistic autonomy, artistic identity, and research capacity in higher art education, and how these relationships might be transformed by artificial intelligence. The research methods are based on a comparative socio-pedagogical approach combining documentary analysis, institutional observation, curriculum analysis, and qualitative interpretation. The empirical component draws primarily on field study conducted in Saint-Étienne, France, during 2024–2025, with particular attention to the École Supérieure d'Art et Design de Saint-Étienne (ESADSE) and Université Jean Monnet, while Armenian higher art education is examined as a comparative context. The analysis is informed by Pierre Bourdieu's concept of cultural production, Michel Foucault's understanding of disciplinary formation, and the concept of artistic research. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the comparative socio-pedagogical analysis of French and Armenian higher art education as distinct educational cultures, in interpreting artistic formation as a movement from disciplinary learning toward increasing autonomy and research capacity, and in extending this framework to the relationship between artistic autonomy and artificial intelligence. The results indicate that both French and Armenian systems recognise the importance of technical and professional competence but organise the transition toward artistic autonomy differently. The French programmes examined show a more explicit progression from foundational education toward specialisation, individual projects, experimentation, professional engagement, and research-oriented practice. Armenian higher art education retains a stronger continuity with systematic technical and disciplinary formation, while incorporating comparable Bachelor–Master–Doctoral structures. Conclusions. Technical competence and artistic autonomy should not be treated as opposing educational objectives; contemporary art education requires a productive transition between disciplinary knowledge and independent creative agency. The emergence of AI further complicates this relationship by shifting attention from technical execution toward conceptual thinking, critical judgement, authorship, research capacity, and ethical responsibility. For Armenian higher art education, the findings suggest an approach based on adaptation rather than imitation, combining established traditions of technical formation with greater opportunities for specialisation, artistic research, professional practice, digital literacy, and responsible human–AI creative engagement.

items.title: From Distant to Dialogic Reading: Large Language Models and the Methodological Reconfiguration of Literary Criticism
items.abstract: This review examines the conceptual architecture and methodological implications of the dialogic reading framework as proposed in "From Distant to Dialogic Reading: Large Language Models and the Methodological Reconfiguration of Literary Criticism." The framework advances a timely intervention in digital literary studies by proposing a shift from the extractive logic of distant reading to a dialogic mode in which large language models function not as instruments of pattern detection but as interlocutors in a recursive hermeneutic process. Situating the framework within the broader scholarly conversation surrounding AI and literary interpretation, this review evaluates its theoretical foundations, methodological rigor, and empirical grounding. The framework draws on Bakhtinian dialogism, Eco's theory of the open work, and the functionalist stance in AI criticism to provide a vocabulary for treating machine-generated interpretations as provocations rather than pronouncements. However, the review argues that while the framework's central thesis offers a productive reconceptualization of computational criticism's aims, its contribution remains primarily programmatic. The absence of controlled comparison, the underspecification of criteria for interpretive value, and the insufficient engagement with critical AI scholarship collectively limit its immediate applicability. The Barthes–Eco Simulation, while pedagogically suggestive, does not demonstrate that dialogic reading produces insights unavailable through conventional methods. The review identifies three requirements for operationalizing dialogic reading as a testable methodology: specifying the conditions under which LLM outputs contribute interpretive surplus rather than algorithmic positivity; developing criteria for evaluating human-machine interpretive collaboration; and conducting controlled comparisons against established methods on common corpora. The hermeneutic hypercycle model offers one promising template for such empirical work. The framework provides the conceptual scaffolding; the harder work of building and testing the structure remains.

items.title: From generative AI usage to entrepreneurial intention: The sequential roles of task and social self-efficacy
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly evolving and creating new possibilities for supporting students' entrepreneurial development. However, limited research has examined how GAI usage is associated with entrepreneurial intention (EI) through specific psychological pathways. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, this study examines the relationship between GAI usage and EI, focusing on the mediating roles of task and social self-efficacy. Using survey data from 521 Chinese university students, this study empirically tests the proposed model. The results show that GAI usage is positively associated with students' task and social self-efficacy. However, task self-efficacy (TSE) is not directly associated with EI. In contrast, social self-efficacy (SSE) accounts for a significant indirect association between GAI usage and EI. Moreover, a significant sequential indirect association is observed, linking GAI usage with EI through TSE and SSE. By disentangling the distinct roles of TSE and SSE, this study shows that the association between GAI usage and EI is consistent with pathways that differ in their functions and proximity to entrepreneurial action. The findings also provide practical insights for entrepreneurship education and AI-supported learning environments.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and innovation performance in emerging-economy SMEs
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is reaching small firms in emerging economies with unusual speed, because it is rented, not built, and is operated through ordinary language instead of code. This paper develops a conceptual framework that explains when and how generative AI use improves innovation performance in emerging-economy small and medium-sized enterprises. Drawing on absorptive capacity, dynamic capabilities and the institution-based view, and on the resource-based view for the diffusion argument, the framework treats generative AI as a low-cost conduit to codified external knowledge whose innovation value depends on the firm's capacity to verify, transform and exploit what the technology produces. Eight propositions, two of them stated as pairs and so ten statements in all, specify the mechanisms and boundary conditions. Generative AI is expected to widen knowledge access most where external knowledge networks are weakest, to strengthen sensing and the design elements of seizing more than transforming, and to favour incremental product and service innovation, process innovation within existing operations, business model innovation and innovation speed over novel product innovation. Its effect is moderated at the firm level by the evaluative expertise of the owner-manager and core staff, and bounded by the type of institutional void the firm faces, by an infrastructure and affordability threshold, by the fit between the model's training data and the firm's language and market context, and by the stage of diffusion among competing firms. As use diffuses, advantage shifts from access to the combination of generative AI with idiosyncratic local knowledge. The paper treats generative AI as a substitute for the channels through which these firms have obtained external knowledge and a complement to the firm's own evaluative expertise, and sets out a research agenda for testing the framework.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence, Academic Integrity and Authentic Assessment within an Irish University
items.abstract: Academics need both an overarching policy on Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) use in teaching and learning, yet agency in its application across various disciplines. Clarity on the use of the technology for both students and staff is therefore a challenge and characterised by uncertainty given how its application is still unfamiliar. This research examines the organisational context in which Gen AI is being embraced and was conducted by the digital teaching support functions within an Irish university. Students and staff were surveyed (n=1,746) on various aspects of digital use within their education and workplace, including Gen AI. This data explored to what extent staff and students are adopting the technology in their work and study, which tools they use and importantly what guidance they received. The university statement of intent identifies that it acknowledges that students and staff are already using AI tools and that it is supportive of the legitimate and appropriate application of such tools once university policies are adhered to. This research probes into the extent that this ambition is achieved on the ground and how guidance is being interpreted while maintaining the integrity of academic work.

items.abstract: Explicit and tacit knowledge are used to describe articulation, practicalexpertise, and learned capabilities, but these uses do not by themselves establisha formal representational boundary. This paper reviews those perspectives anddevelops a conditional criterion for recovering a comparison system’sExplicit/Tacit classification. On a nonempty semantic domain, a representationpreserves a target exactly when equal representation values imply equal targetvalues. An independently specified correctness family determines a canonicalquotient, while a qualifying representation regime determines which selectedcontents are representable. A typed interpretation fixes the comparison domain.Two correctness inclusions and two representation-spectrum inclusions, togetherwith the comparison system’s modal characterizations, imply agreement of theclassifications on that domain. A finite safety-and-authorization exampleestablishes all four conditions, shows that both classes are nonempty, andsupplies counterexamples to each alignment condition. The analysis distinguishesfinite naming from faithful representation, individual from aggregaterepresentability, and informational from operational recovery. Admission of acriterion can invalidate an adequate representation; a case interpretation showswhen its distinction also refines Paper I’s task requirements. Architecturalconsequences require Paper I’s independent contract conditions. Lean verifies theneutral core, conditional recovery, domain restriction, and finite comparison; thecriterion-to-task interpretation is a manuscript-level argument. The resultprovides application-specific proof obligations without establishing universal Tacitnonemptiness, human-exclusive realization, or principalhood.

items.title: Graph-based misinformation detection: a comprehensive survey of representations, learning methods, datasets, and future directions
items.abstract: Misinformation refers to false, inaccurate, or misleading information that can significantly influence public opinion, decision-making, and societal behaviour. With the rapid growth of social media and online communication platforms, the large-scale dissemination of misinformation has become a critical challenge, highlighting the need for effective automated detection techniques. This survey presents a comprehensive review of recent advances in misinformation detection by examining the complete detection pipeline, including information representation, event detection, semantic similarity analysis, information verification, and classification methods. It reviews conventional machine learning, deep learning, graph-based, and transformer-based approaches that have been proposed for identifying misinformation across diverse application domains. Furthermore, widely used benchmark datasets are analysed, and the performance characteristics of representative detection models are compared to highlight their strengths and limitations. The survey also identifies current research challenges, including data quality, explainability, domain adaptation, multimodal misinformation, and model generalisation, and discusses promising future research directions. By providing a structured overview of existing methodologies, datasets, and emerging trends, this survey serves as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners working in misinformation detection and trustworthy artificial intelligence.

items.title: GraphLLM4CTR: Large Language Model-Enhanced Graph Neural Networks for Click-through Rate Prediction in Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a crucial task to estimate the probability that users will click on items in online platforms. Recently, researchers have incorporated semantics derived from large language models (LLMs) into representations of users and items in graph neural networks (GNNs) framework to facilitate CTR prediction. However, existing hybrid GNNs-LLMs models predominantly treat GNNs and LLMs as two independent components, and suffer from the ineffective modality alignment between graph and textual representations. To address these issues, we propose LLMs-enhanced GNNs for CTR prediction (GraphLLM4CTR), where LLMs coordinate message passing in GNNs by infusing layer-wise semantics into message updates and graph representation learning. Specifically, we design a multi-view contrastive alignment (MVCA) method to transform graph and prompt-based embeddings into modality-aware representations and achieve modality alignment through intra-view and inter-view contrastive learning. Moreover, we propose a LLMs-based message coordinator (LBMC) that projects graph representations into an aligned latent space and incorporates LLMs with learnable adapters to regulate semantic-injected graph representation learning. Subsequently, we present a hybrid-expert mechanism with gating networks to adaptively aggregate representations for CTR prediction. Experiments conducted on three public datasets (i.e., MovieLens-1M, BookCrossing, and Amazon-Sports) demonstrate the superiority of GraphLLM4CTR over state-of-the-art baselines in terms of AUC and Logloss, and validate the adaptability of MVCA to topological properties and of LBMC to text qualities, and the dynamic balance of the hybrid-expert mechanism. Finally, we conduct analysis of space and time complexity, and computational efficiency of GraphLLM4CTR during training and inference stages, which indicates that GraphLLM4CTR can achieve the optimal AUC-latency trade-off and a linear scalability with the number of nodes and of edges in constructed graphs.

items.title: Green retrofitting in ceramics manufacturing industry: a hybrid LLM-MCDM approach
items.abstract: This study examines strategic retrofitting in high-end artistic ceramics manufacturing under stringent “Dual Carbon” regulations. Balancing regulatory compliance with artisanal integrity represents a significant industrial challenge. To address this multidimensional problem, this research develops an integrated hybrid multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) framework combining the Full Consistency Method (FUCOM) and the Measurement of Alternatives and Ranking according to Compromise Solution (MARCOS). Gemini 1.5 Pro was employed exclusively as a “Synthetic Knowledge Engineer” to extract and organise candidate criteria from five authoritative regulatory and technical documents, which were subsequently validated and refined by a multidisciplinary human expert panel to construct the Evaluation Index System (EIS). FUCOM results indicate that “Environmental Compliance and Process Monitoring” is the most influential main criterion, while “Specific Energy Intensity”, “Weighted Flue Gas Emissions” and “Payback Period and ROI” emerge as the most important sub-criteria. The MARCOS evaluation identifies the “Hybrid Evolutionary Path” as the highest-ranked compromise pathway, reflecting a phased investment strategy that balances emission reduction objectives with capital constraints. Sensitivity analyses and comparative assessments using established MCDM methods, including TOPSIS, COPRAS, WASPAS and VIKOR, demonstrate a high degree of ranking stability under the tested analytical conditions. The proposed framework provides a transparent and potentially transferable decision-support approach to facilitate low-carbon transitions in traditional craft-based manufacturing industries.

items.title: Hazard Exposure, Knowledge and Safety Practices among Healthcare Workers in Primary Healthcare Centres in Port Harcourt, Nigeria: A Cross-sectional Study
items.abstract: Background: Occupational hazards remain an important concern among healthcare workers, particularly in resource-limited primary healthcare settings where inadequate protective equipment, heavy workloads and limited occupational health support may increase exposure risks. Although healthcare workers may have good knowledge of occupational hazards, this knowledge does not always translate into consistent safety practices. Evidence on this knowledge–practice gap among primary healthcare workers in Nigeria remains limited. Aims: To assess occupational hazard exposure, knowledge of occupational hazards and safety practices among healthcare workers in primary healthcare centres, and to examine whether the level of hazard exposure was associated with the level of safety practice. Study Design: Descriptive cross-sectional study. Place and Duration of Study: Two government-owned primary healthcare centres in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, Nigeria, between April 2026 and June 2026. Methodology: A structured self-administered questionnaire was completed by 124 clinical and non-clinical healthcare workers selected by proportionate allocation and simple random sampling. Hazard exposure, knowledge and safety practice were measured on five-point Likert scales and classified from composite scores. The association between exposure level and practice level was tested with Pearson’s chi-square and the Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact test. Results: Most respondents were female (64.5%) and aged 45 years or older (51.6%). Exposure was reported across all hazard categories; 71.0% agreed that they had experienced a needlestick or sharps injury, 64.5% reported exposure to blood or body fluids, and 61.3% reported work-related stress. Overall, 62.1% had high hazard exposure. Knowledge was good in 97.6% of respondents, yet only 16.1% agreed that they consistently used personal protective equipment and 18.5% that they regularly practised hand hygiene. Overall, 79.0% had fair and 15.3% good safety practice. Heavy workload was the most strongly endorsed barrier (58.1% agreement). Safety practice level was not associated with hazard exposure level (χ² = 2.383, df = 2, p = 0.304; exact p = 0.316). Conclusion: Healthcare workers in these centres knew the risks well but did not consistently apply basic protective measures, and workers with high exposure practised no more safely than those with moderate exposure. Improving safety in primary care is therefore likely to depend on equipment supply, staffing and supportive supervision more than on further awareness training.

items.title: Hierarchical Credit Assignment for RLVR on Fused Gromov-Wasserstein Geometry
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has been shown to improve the reasoning capability of large language models (LLMs) across diverse reasoning tasks. However, group-based RLVR methods, such as GRPO, assign a uniform advantage to all tokens within rollouts of the same outcome. While existing works refine credit assignment of GRPO based on local signals such as token locations or entropy, they often fail to capture the global semantic novelty of a reasoning behavior relative to the current policy. In this work, we propose a hierarchical credit assignment approach for group-based RLVR methods, called HarA, which identifies and encourages semantically novel reasoning behaviors during RLVR. HarA represents each sampled rollout as a distribution over the hidden states and locations of tokens, and computes the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) barycenters of all rollouts with the same outcome, capturing the internal reasoning patterns in the latent space under the current policy. The semantic novelty of a reasoning element can then be measured by its contribution to the FGW distance between the current rollout and the barycenter. While solving the FGW formulation is expensive, we introduce an anchor-guided linearization that turns it into a Wasserstein formulation solvable via the Sinkhorn algorithm efficiently. By reweighing token-level advantage of group-based RLVR methods based on the novelty signals, HarA highlights novel reasoning behaviors at flexible granularities to encourage fine-grained LLM exploration. Extensive experiments across three group-based RLVR methods show that our plug-and-play method effectively enhances the exploration of LLMs, outperforming existing methods across diverse reasoning benchmarks.

items.title: How can empowering leadership foster employee–AI collaboration? A multilevel analysis of AI trust and psychological safety
items.abstract: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the workplace underscores the urgent need to understand how employees collaborate effectively with AI systems. Grounded in social cognitive theory, this study investigates the impact of empowering leadership on employee–AI collaboration. Furthermore, we examine the mediating roles of psychological safety and AI trust. Design/methodology/approach To test the research model, we utilized a multilevel design data from 418 employees across 103 teams in AI-integrated organizations in Vietnam. Findings Our findings indicate that empowering leadership is positively related to employee–AI collaboration, with this relationship mediated by both psychological safety and AI trust. Originality/value This study contributes to the leadership and technology management literature by establishing a multilevel link between empowering leadership and employee–AI collaboration. It identifies key mediating mechanisms (AI trust and psychological safety), offering a more integrated understanding of leadership influence in AI-enabled settings. Practically, the findings offer actionable insights for practitioners navigating the dynamics of employee–AI collaboration, highlighting the importance of empowering leadership in building AI-ready workforces.

items.title: How conversational AI shapes the readability of 10-K reports
items.abstract: Purpose We investigate whether the adoption of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) translates corporate complexity into clearer financial narratives. CAI, representing AI-driven innovation, can bolster operational efficiency and performance, thereby leading to better financial transparency and readability of financial statement information. Design/methodology/approach We construct a firm-level CAI measure from CAI-related disclosures in 10-K filings using Sent-latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA)-variational expectation maximization (VEM) topic modelling. Our measure captures CAI applications related to service and operations, and decision-making and governance. We also use patent-based measures based on natural language processing and speech-recognition technologies as alternative proxies in robustness tests. Findings We find that CAI adoption is associated with lower Bog Index scores, indicating more readable 10-K reports. Mediation tests show that financial performance and operational efficiency partially mediate this relationship. The results remain robust after addressing endogeneity concerns and using alternative specifications. Originality/value Using unsupervised machine learning topic modelling, we observe that CAI is predominantly employed in corporate operations, notably in service-related activities, decision-making processes and corporate governance.

items.title: How modified flipped learning affects pre-service teachers’ learning motivation, flow experience and collaborative problem solving process
items.abstract: Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) constitutes an important competence for pre-service teachers. However, fostering their deep engagement in such tasks remains a persistent challenge. Drawing upon self-determination theory and flow theory, the present study introduced an innovative gamification mechanism into a university classroom and integrated it with the flipped classroom approach. A nine-week quasi-experiment was implemented with 40 pre-service teachers in China. Data were collected through pre- and post-intervention surveys on learning motivation and flow experience and video recordings of collaborative sessions. Quantitative data were analysed using paired-samples t-tests, while video data were examined using Lag Sequential Analysis (LSA) to identify significant behavioural transitions in the CPS process. Results showed that intrinsic motivation and flow significantly improved. LSA revealed that CPS patterns evolved positively under game elements, including more efficient knowledge construction, more critical solution testing and more effective social interactions. Limitations and future directions are discussed.

items.title: How RL Reshapes LLM Reasoning: Transferability, Coverage, and Scaling Laws
items.abstract: Recent studies on reinforcement learning (RL) report seemingly conflicting evidence about large language model (LLM) reasoning. Training on mathematics can improve performance in other domains, yet gains in Pass@1 can coincide with lower Pass@$N$ than the base model. This raises a fundamental question: does RL expand an LLM's reasoning boundary, or merely reweight its existing reasoning space? We revisit these phenomena across Qwen and Gemma model families, showing both cross-domain gains and forgetting, while coverage at large sampling budgets increases on some tasks and decreases on others. Detailed analysis of solution traces before and after RL indicates a shift in the reasoning strategies the model employs, motivating a two-stage autoregressive policy model that separates \emph{strategy selection} from problem-specific execution. Within this framework, we prove how RL's implicit bias reshapes strategy preferences, allowing gains on some tasks while suppressing strategies required by others. This mechanism can also broaden or narrow coverage at a given sampling budget even without expanding strategy support. We further provide theoretical justifications for log-sigmoid and log-linear scaling laws in RL compute, and evaluate their predictive power. Together, these results connect changes in strategy selection to cross-domain transfer, reasoning coverage, and compute scaling.

items.title: Human Behavior-Informed Crash Scenario Generation with Real-World Crash Priors for Autonomous Vehicle Safety Evaluation
items.abstract: Reliable safety evaluation of autonomous vehicles (AVs) is essential to improving road safety, yet it depends critically on realistic simulation of rare crashes. Existing crash scenario generation methods can increase collision occurrence, but often fail to realistically reproduce how crashes evolve before impact or the distribution of crash types observed in the real world. Here, we present CrashSim, a human behavior-informed crash scenario generation framework that uses real-world crash priors to guide generative multi-agent traffic simulation for more reliable AV safety evaluation. These priors capture how real-world crashes evolve before impact and how different crash types are distributed, allowing limited crash data to guide realistic and scalable scenario generation across naturalistic driving contexts. We evaluate CrashSim against competing methods, showing that it more closely reproduces real-world pre-impact behavior, collision dynamics, collision geometry and crash-type distributions. We further use CrashSim to construct nuCrash dataset, containing over 4,000 crash and near-crash scenarios. Closed-loop evaluation of five AV planners shows that nuCrash more effectively exposes differences in planner safety capabilities than nuScenes. An LLM-assisted evaluation agent further analyzes planner failures to provide capability-level diagnoses and targeted improvement guidance. Together, CrashSim enables realistic and scalable crash generation for more informative AV safety evaluation.

items.title: Human Factors in Brain–Computer Interfaces: Boundaries, Key Issues, and Methodological Approaches
items.abstract: The large-scale, real-world deployment of brain–computer interface (BCI) is confronted with human factors bottlenecks, including reliability and usability. While modern human factors engineering has encompassed domains such as cognitive ergonomics, workload, adaptive automation, and human-in-the-loop systems, its theories and methodologies have historically placed their main emphasis on overt behavior and peripheral physiological measures, rather than on central neural activity as a primary control input. For the emerging interaction paradigm that takes central nervous activity as direct input and emphasizes long-term brain–computer co-adaptation, there remains a shortage of targeted conceptual and methodological frameworks. As a conceptual review, this paper discusses the necessity and disciplinary foundations for developing Human Factors Engineering for BCIs as an emerging interdisciplinary research direction. First, grounded in the defining features of BCI interaction—such as the implicit nature of input and brain–computer co-adaptation—it delineates the research boundaries and summarizes the core research objects as user neurocognitive characteristics, brain–computer collaborative adaptation mechanisms, multimodal feedback regulation, and contextual adaptation patterns. Second, it identifies three core scientific questions: individual differences and dynamic adaptation, human factors optimization and fault tolerance, and contextual generalizability principles, with ethics, privacy, and user rights and interests as an overarching dimension. Furthermore, it constructs a methodological system consisting of multimodal measurement and modeling, closed-loop validation, and multidimensional evaluation, and examines the supporting role of artificial intelligence approaches within this framework. Centered on the collaborative adaptation across neural, cognitive, and system levels, Human Factors Engineering for BCIs represents a deepening of the human-centered design philosophy. It provides theoretical reference for user-friendly BCI design and extends the research boundaries of human factors engineering.

items.title: Human Genuine Intelligence in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is increasingly capable of performing cognitive work that was previously associated primarily with human intellectual ability. Generative AI can now assist with writing, analysis, reasoning, coding, interpretation, and decision support, allowing individuals to produce sophisticated intellectual outputs that may exceed their independently demonstrated understanding. As a result, the quality of human output may become an increasingly incomplete indicator of the cognitive capability genuinely possessed by the human producing it.This conceptual opinion paper proposes Human Genuine Intelligence (HGI) as a framework for examining this emerging distinction. HGI refers to the cognitive capacity that humans genuinely possess, understand, and exercise through question formation, independent reasoning, analytical thinking, evidence evaluation, causal understanding, judgment, and cognitive revision.The paper introduces Borrowed Intelligence (BI) and the Cognitive Dependency Gap (CDG) as conceptual lenses for examining potential mismatches between AI-augmented capability and independently accountable human cognitive capability. Rather than advocating reduced use of AI, it proposes Active Cognitive Augmentation (ACA) as a model for human–AI interaction: THINK → ASK → AUGMENT → CHALLENGE → VERIFY → REVISE → DECIDE WITH WISDOM.The paper further argues that cognitive capability alone is insufficient for navigating increasingly powerful AI systems. HGI therefore needs to be considered alongside Human Wisdom, which provides direction and responsibility, and Cognitive Sovereignty, which concerns the preservation of human agency and authority over consequential goals, values, delegation boundaries, and decisions.The central challenge of the AI age is therefore not to preserve human intelligence by limiting artificial intelligence, but to strengthen human cognition, wisdom, and agency while using increasingly capable machines.

items.abstract: AI incident databases and risk taxonomies are increasingly valuable, but they often answer broad questions about harm, misuse, or system failure rather than the narrower operational question of whether humans remain meaningfully in control of increasingly agentic systems. This paper proposes the Human Control Model, a six-dimension framework for analyzing agent-control failures: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. The framework separates behavioral severity from environment reality so that controlled evaluations are not presented as real-world incidents. This v1.1 revision updates the paper title to better distinguish the work while preserving the Human in Control project name, the existing Human Control Model, the six-dimension framework, the original version lineage, and the publication record family. The framework is conceptual and case-based, without inter-rater reliability testing or validated quantitative thresholds. The prepared local export updates the recoverable v1.0.1 manuscript title and metadata; the prior longer sandbox-only v1.1 manuscript was unavailable. Creator: Human in Control Project. items.title: Human, Organisational, and Navigational Factors in Selected North Sea Ship Collisions: A Qualitative Comparative Case Study
items.abstract: Ship collisions in the North Sea remain a significant maritime safety concern because the region combines merchant traffic, fishing activity, offshore operations, and traffic separation schemes. This study examines five purposively selected North Sea ship collisions occurring between 2010 and 2023 to identify recurring human, organisational, and navigational factors and develop practical lessons for reducing collision risk. A qualitative comparative case-study approach was employed using official Marine Accident Investigation Branch and Dutch Safety Board reports. Documentary analysis and thematic coding covered 22 factors across five cases. The most consistently supported weaknesses concerned lookout and monitoring, situation awareness, risk of collision assessment, and electronic navigational information. Communication, bridge redundancy, and organisational controls also showed deficiencies, although their form and evidential support differed. Evidence concerning fatigue and some organisational explanations was qualified. The cross-case interpretation identified erosion of overlapping safety barriers before impact, while recognising functioning safeguards and limitations in the report evidence. The findings support recommendations for observable watchkeeping standards, effective technology use, bridge-team support, fatigue-aware operations, and organisational verification. These conclusions concern the selected cases and do not establish the frequency or causal strength of the factors across all North Sea collisions.

items.title: Ideological Stance Detection in a Low-Resource Language: Polarization in Bangladeshi Public vs Private University Discourse on Social Media
items.abstract: Public vs. private universities is a debatable issue, and it creates polarization on social media in Bangladesh. Debate on quality, jobs, and prestige is passionate among the students, parents, and graduates, the majority of whom speak Bengali, a low-resource language. To measure this polarization, this paper introduces a manually annotated dataset of 4,060 Bengali comments labeled as Pro-Public, Pro-Private, or Neutral. We evaluated the quality of our annotations by Fleiss's Kappa agreement that was 0.89, corresponding to a high agreement among annotators. The classical ML (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost), BiLSTM network, hybrid BanglaBERT+XGBoost models and the state-of-the-art zero-shot LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-V3.1, Llama 4 Maverick, Kimi K2 Thinking, Qwen3-235B Thinking) models are evaluated. The accuracy of BanglaBERT+XGBoost is 91.81% and macro F1 score is 91.70%, which is higher than all the supervised baselines. The zero-shot Llama 4 Maverick Thinking achieves a macro F1 of 0.931 (overall accuracy of 93.31%) without any fine-tuning. All machine learning (ML), deep machine learning (DL) and transformer models were outperformed by the zero-shot Llama 4 Maverick model. Polarization also is evident, in some ways more clearly in the Pro-Private comments, which emphasize modern facilities and timely graduation, versus the Pro-Public comments, which emphasize affordability and government jobs. Our findings open new directions for analyzing social media polarization in low-resource languages.

items.title: Impact of AI-Based Financial Advice on Investment Preferences and Risk Perception among Salaried Investors
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to deliver financial information, investment recommendations and portfolio decision support. This study examines the proposed impact of AI-based financial advice on investment preferences and risk perception among salaried investors. The framework treats perceived usefulness, perceived accuracy, trust, personalisation and transparency as dimensions of AI-based financial advice and tests their proposed relationships with investment preference and risk perception. A quantitative cross-sectional design using a structured five-point Likert questionnaire is proposed. For demonstration of the intended empirical reporting format, a synthetic dataset of 450 hypothetical salaried investors was generated and analysed using internal-consistency assessment and regression-style structural estimates. The simulated results indicate positive associations between the five AI-advice attributes and investment preference and negative associations with risk perception. These numerical findings are illustrative only and must not be represented as observations from real respondents. The study contributes a focused framework for future primary research on AI-assisted investment decision-making among salaried investors.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Tools on the Learning Behaviour and Academic Engagement of Generation Z Students
items.abstract: Abstract It is evident that Artificial Intelligence (AI) now plays and important role in every students life. It is being adapted progressively becoming an inevitable part of almost every student’s academic performance. The use of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Canva, and many more AI-based learning platforms support student learning effectively. These tools aid as search engine machines used to extract information. Students often use AI learning based platforms for synthezising challenging concepts, seeking creative assignment ideas. They also use AI tools for taming writing skills and specifically during preparation of their exam preparation. Generation Z, is known to be digitally native so they have grown up in an environment which is highly digital in nature. So they are highly privileged to secure an environment that not only supports but also openly accepts wide usage of AI based technologies. This adoption of AI based technology learning not only designs their day to day living easy, but also supports them in their learning processes. AI tools facilitate learning quicker in less time and features personalised learning. AI based learning tools are easily accessible for students as they are either free of cost or offered to students at lower costs. Although excessive dependence on AI based tools for learning is not fit for students as, it restricts their independent critical thinking blocking their creativity minds and hinders problem-solving abilities. The main purpose of the research paper was to scrutinize the impact of AI tools on the learning behaviour of Gen Z students. The study is an attempt to focus on gauging the frequency with which the Gen Z students use AI learning tools, understanding the purpose of AI usage. An analysis is done through to pivot lenses on the influence of AI based learning on various parameters like learning efficiency, change academic engagement, and the perception of students. It will give a clear picture whether students hold AI based learning as an advantage or a possible limitation when adopted for educational purposes.

items.title: Improving clinical data standardization in surgical notes through biomedical entity linking with contextual evidence from large language models
items.abstract: Surgical notes contain essential clinical information for postoperative care, yet free-text format and institutional variability limit their use for standardized data representation and secondary analysis. Biomedical entity linking enables mapping of heterogeneous clinical expressions to standardized ontologies such as SNOMED-CT, supporting semantic interoperability. However, existing approaches often rely on predefined mention spans through named entity recognition (NER), which is labor-intensive and may introduce errors. We analyzed 9,051 gastric cancer surgical notes from Seoul National University Hospital. We developed a framework that leverages an open-source large language model (LLM; LLaMA-3.1-8B) to identify contextually relevant text segments, termed evidence spans, which provide cues for ontology-based entity linking. These spans were explicitly marked and used to fine-tune SapBERT, a pretrained embedding-based biomedical encoder. We compared multiple input variants against conventional pipelines and LLM-based approaches, including in-context learning and re-ranking. Incorporating evidence spans improved entity linking performance across metrics, with gains of +2.7 in Recall@1 and +2.2 in mean Average Precision at 3 (mAP@3) compared to raw text inputs. Evidence-guided models outperformed other LLM-based approaches, with additional gains when using the evidence marker token as the pooled representation. Attention analysis indicated that explicit evidence span marking reinforced the model’s focus on ontology-relevant context while reducing attention to irrelevant text. Leveraging LLM-derived contextual evidence improves ontology-based representation of clinical text by enhancing biomedical entity linking. This approach provides a practical strategy for standardizing unstructured surgical notes and supports more reliable secondary use of clinical data in real-world healthcare settings. More broadly, the framework supports mapping of unstructured clinical text to standardized ontologies, contributing to semantic interoperability and enabling downstream secondary use of clinical data.

items.title: Instructional Design in Social Science Education with AI Co-Design Approach
items.abstract: This record serves as a living document for a 12-session course titled "Instructional Design in Social Science Education with AI Co-Design Approach," delivered at Farhangian University (Tehran, Iran) during the 2025–2026 academic year. The course transforms pre-service social science teachers from passive consumers of curriculum into active "architects of learning environments" through the integration of Generative AI into instructional design. It equips student-teachers with the competencies needed to design, evaluate, and redesign instructional materials that are pedagogically sound, contextually grounded, and resistant to uncritical AI substitution. The course comprises twelve interconnected lesson packages, each containing: (1) a classical instructional design source, summarized as a Persian-language module with theoretical foundations and practical examples; (2) an avant-garde AI-related article exploring emerging research and applications in AI-mediated education; and (3) a structured prompt toolkit enabling student-teachers to co-design instruction with generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek. The course follows a three-stage progression: • Critical Exploration — using AI to surface the limitations of traditional linear instructional models and to identify their epistemological assumptions; • Co-Design Synthesis — applying the Integrated AI Triad (IAT) framework to co-create lesson plans and redesign passive curriculum units with a focus on authentic, context-anchored learning; • Reflective Validation — documenting design decisions through structured prompts, blind peer adjudication, and reflective journaling. Twelve thematic sessions cover: the foundations of instructional design; learning theories and AI; problem definition; needs assessment; learning outcomes; content redesign; strategies for concepts and procedures; principles and causal relationships; higher-order thinking; assessment design; interactive message design; and reflective synthesis. Course outputs include 29 redesigned lesson plans from three national sociology textbooks (Sociology 1, Sociology 2, and Sociology 3), developed collaboratively by 29 student-teacher teams. All redesigned lessons are released as an open dataset to support reproducible research in AI-mediated instructional design. This record is updated weekly throughout the semester. Each update adds the lesson package corresponding to the current session. The Concept DOI remains constant, ensuring a single persistent link for the entire course.

The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and cybersecurity has intensified concerns about the opacity of complex models, which undermines stakeholder trust and slows adoption. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses this by producing justifications for model decisions, yet such justifications are typically delivered as raw textual or numerical output that many stakeholders find difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that integrates XAI with advanced data visualization, treating visualization as a first-class layer of the explanation pipeline rather than an afterthought: post-hoc attribution methods supply explanation content, and purpose-designed visual encodings — heatmaps, feature-importance dashboards, and decision-path graphs — supply a cognitively efficient form. Beyond the framework, the paper specifies a standardized, falsifiable evaluation protocol spanning three benchmark domains and seven measurable constructs — explanation satisfaction, objective understanding, decision accuracy, cognitive load, subjective trust, calibrated trust, and decision confidence — with directional hypotheses grounded in perceptual and cognitive-explanation theory. A structured results-reporting design is included to support immediate empirical application. The primary contribution is the framework, the measurement standard, and the evaluation protocol.

items.title: INTEGRATING PROBLEM-BASED LEARNING AND DEEP LEARNING TO ENHANCE MATHEMATICAL REASONING AMONG JUNIOR HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS: A ONE-GROUP PRETEST–POSTTEST QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL STUDY
items.abstract: AbstractMathematical reasoning is a fundamental competency in contemporary mathematics education, yet many junior high school students continue to experience difficulties in constructing logical arguments, connecting mathematical concepts, and solving complex problems. This study examined changes in junior high school students' mathematical reasoning following the implementation of Problem-Based Learning (PBL) integrated with a Deep Learning approach. A quantitative one-group pretest–posttest quasi-experimental design was employed involving 30 Grade VIII students from a public junior high school in North Sumatra, Indonesia. The instructional intervention was implemented across four mathematics learning sessions on Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables to promote meaningful learning, reflective thinking, and active problem solving. Data were collected using a validated mathematical reasoning test administered before and after the intervention. Descriptive statistics, the Kolmogorov–Smirnov normality test, paired-sample t-test, and N-Gain analysis were used. The findings revealed a statistically significant improvement in students' mathematical reasoning following the instructional intervention, with mean scores increasing from 41.73 in the pretest to 79.40 in the posttest (t(29) = 18.063, p < .001, Cohen's d = 3.30). Because the study employed a one-group pretest–posttest design, these findings indicate substantial within-group improvement following the intervention rather than definitive evidence of causal effectiveness. The mean N-Gain score of 0.64 indicated a moderate level of improvement. The results suggest that integrating PBL with a Deep Learning approach is associated with improvements in mathematical reasoning. The study contributes to innovative mathematics instruction and offers practical implications for improving teaching and learning in education. His research interests include mathematics education, STEM education, problem-based learning, mathematical reasoning, ethnomathematics, digital learning, artificial intelligence in education, and assessment for learning. He has teaching experience at both secondary and higher education levels and actively contributes to academic publications, conferences, and peer review activities. items.title: Interpretable multimodal retrieval augmented diagnosis for breast ultrasound with multinational clinical validation and reader study
items.abstract: Breast ultrasound is central to breast cancer diagnosis but suffers from substantial inter-observer variability in Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) assessment, and existing deep learning models remain opaque. Multimodal large language models promise interpretable report-based reasoning, yet scarce paired image-report data yields weak visual-semantic alignment. We propose B-RAD, a BI-RADS-aware retrieval-augmented diagnosis framework that mirrors the radiologist workflow of retrieving exemplars, localizing lesions, and determining the BI-RADS category. Its retrieval module learns BI-RADS-aware alignment from unpaired data by jointly minimizing cross-modal mismatch and ordinal prediction error. Retrieved exemplars guide few-shot detection of the lesion together with its margin and posterior acoustic features, and the detected region prompts a segmentation model whose mask drives training-free foveal attention for classification. We validated B-RAD on eleven cohorts from seven countries totaling 8311 images, spanning internal validation and three external cohorts including an independent institutional cohort. The full pipeline reached a biopsy triage AUROC of 0.952 on that institutional cohort without fine-tuning, outperforming existing vision-language models. In a four-reader study, B-RAD assistance improved accuracy, raised inter-reader agreement from moderate to substantial, and reduced missed malignancies across all readers. These findings show that retrieval-augmented diagnosis can narrow the expertise gap and support accessible breast cancer screening in resource-limited settings.

items.title: Intervention-Disclosure Visibility and Time-Bounded Selective Nondisclosure in Hierarchical Agent Systems
items.abstract: Within Soft and Hard De-Attraction (SHDA), this paper treats intervention disclosure in persistent-state artificial agents as an observer-field-channel-time contract. It separates assignment, valid delivery, existence awareness and field knowledge, records missing measurement as UNKNOWN, and distinguishes disclosure-policy from awareness-mediated effects, whose natural forms need further identifying assumptions. By Proposition W1, field knowledge is monotone under joins of views and retained histories but cannot be certified view by view. Building on the elementary direction of Blackwell's comparison of experiments, Proposition W2 bounds an evaluator's one-shot benefit from withholding by departures from common loss, optimal response, free imitation, an exogenous environment and garbling on the complete evidence, each to be estimated or bounded. Under Proposition W3, a linearizable family ledger bounds authorized, not actual, nondisclosure duration and renewals by the admitting constraints' caps across splits, merges and reclassifications. The paper specifies witness-bound nondisclosure authorization with stable semantic families and persistent obligations, release checks against combined histories, and unexecuted efficacy protocols. Finite-state checks of frozen ledger rules instantiate family accounting and obligation persistence under revision, split/merge and partial or uncertain effect outcomes; without exposure or knowledge state, they retain overcommitted and overdue histories but prove neither timely fulfillment nor usefulness. The contribution is a typed governance interface over established information, missing-data, estimand, auditing and logging results, not a universally optimal disclosure mode, deployed-system safety or permission to conceal interventions from or on humans. Note on Version 2.0. This version replaces Version 1.0 (September 2026; about 9,100 words) and is a substantial revision (about 23,500 words). It adds Propositions W1 to W3 (field knowledge under joins of views, a bound on the one-shot benefit of withholding, and family-ledger caps on authorized nondisclosure), witness-bound nondisclosure authorization, release checks against combined histories and finite-state checks of frozen ledger rules. Files: the manuscript as PDF and a supplement archive (17 files) with the exact mathematical and finite governance checks, the family re-enumeration cited in the paper and the protocol witnesses; the full shared validation reports are in the supplement of the flagship record. The Version 1.0 file remains available in the previous version of this record. Publication role. Companion B develops the disclosure and obligation branch of the Integrated Framework series on contract-preserving lower-to-upper recalibration (SHDA). The flagship and its Technical Supplement are archived separately, as are Companion A on residual genesis and dynamic feedback route attribution, Companion C on family-scoped capability control, typed lineage and atomic re-entry, and the technical working paper SHDA Algorithms for Scoped Evidence Reuse and Recalibration. The formal scope is artificial agent systems; the selection rules do not apply to undisclosed interventions on humans, which require separate consent, rights, and legal and ethical review. No deployment result is reported. AI use disclosure. Generative AI (GPT-6.0, OpenAI; Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used substantively in preparing this work, including source comparison, drafting and editing, and, where applicable, mathematical and counterexample checks and the writing and running of supplementary code. The research questions, framework and final claims were directed and reviewed by the author, who takes full responsibility for the content, including the accuracy of all references and reported numbers. items.title: INVESTIGACIÓN VIVA
items.abstract: Living Research: Understanding Experience to Transform Reality introduces an original methodological and interpretive framework within contemporary qualitative research that integrates phenomenology and action research. The work posits that scientific inquiry is not complete merely by understanding a phenomenon, but when the constructed knowledge returns to its context to enable transformative and reflective action. The author presents conceptual and practical tools such as Experiential Depth, Living Data, Living Units of Meaning, the Living Map of Experience (LME), the Living Phenomenological Understanding Route (LPUR), the Living Transformation Cycle (LTC), and the Transforming Evidence Matrix (TEM). Furthermore, it establishes the principle of Human Interpretive Sovereignty regarding artificial intelligence, defining AI as an operational assistant while upholding that final meaning attribution and ethical responsibility strictly reside within human critical judgment.

items.title: Jerome and the demons of space: Atmospheres from wilderness to intimacy, from the expanse to claustrophilia
items.abstract: This essay examines the relationship between architectural space and affective atmosphere through depictions of Saint Jerome. Applying the phenomenology of atmospheres, it traces Jerome's spatial progression from the agoraphobic, daemon-haunted desert to the serene, enclosed studiolo. This shift is framed as a movement toward claustrophilia—a predilection for intimate space that facilitates focus. Central to the argument is the concept of "affective scaffolding." Jerome's study is a curated material ensemble that filters chaotic external atmospheres, cultivating an artificial climate for intellectual labor. This reveals how subjects manipulate environments to manage feelings, a practice echoing dwelling as the "cultivation of atmospheres." The essay contrasts this pre-modern atmospheric curation with modern ergonomic standardization, which often prioritizes physical efficiency over affective resonance. Ultimately, Jerome’s iconography demonstrates that atmosphere arises from the confluence of environment and corporeal disposition. His retreat shows architecture's power lies not only in form but also in its ability to recede, creating a protective darkness for claustrophilic expansion. Attending to these dynamics is essential for understanding spatial experience beyond the modernist privileging of light and expanse.

items.title: Judgment Formation in AI-Mediated Inquiry: A Preliminary Generative Relational Account
items.abstract: This paper develops a preliminary Generative Relational (GR) account of judgment formation in AI-mediated inquiry. Its analytical object is not judgment in general and not a contest between human and artificial judgment. The paper examines how historically developed capacities for framing, discrimination, confidence calibration, selective reliance, revision, responsibility, and learning are reorganized when artificial intelligence can participate in generating options, reasons, evaluations, recommendations, and polished answers. The starting distinction is between improved task performance and the development of judgment. items.abstract: Résumé Cette étude analyse les facteurs qui influencent l’adoption de l’intelligence artificielle dans l’enseignement supérieur au Maroc ainsi que l’intention des étudiants de l’utiliser dans le futur. Elle s’intéresse notamment au soutien à l’apprentissage, à l’aide à la rédaction, à la productivité, aux pratiques de substitution, à la dépendance et à l’autonomie numérique. L’étude repose sur une approche quantitative menée auprès de 303 étudiants. Les données ont été analysées à l’aide d’une analyse factorielle exploratoire, d’une analyse factorielle confirmatoire et d’un modèle d’équations structurelles. Les résultats montrent que le soutien à l’apprentissage et l’aide à la rédaction influencent positivement l’attitude des étudiants envers l’IA. La productivité et l’attitude influencent également positivement l’intention d’usage futur, tandis que la dépendance exerce une influence négative et significative. En revanche, la relation entre les pratiques de substitution et l’intention d’usage n’est pas significative. Ces résultats montrent que les étudiants considèrent principalement l’IA comme un outil de soutien à leur apprentissage et à leur travail académique, tout en restant conscients des risques liés à une utilisation excessive. Mots-clés : Intelligence artificielle ; enseignement supérieur ; adoption ; intention d’usage ; étudiants ; soutien à l’apprentissage . Abstract This study examines the factors influencing the adoption of artificial intelligence in Moroccan higher education and students’ intention to use it in the future. It focuses on learning support, writing assistance, productivity, substitution practices, dependence, and digital autonomy. The study follows a quantitative approach based on 303 students. The data were analyzed using exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modeling. The results show that learning support and writing assistance have a positive effect on students’ attitudes toward AI. Productivity and attitude also have a positive effect on future use intention, while dependence has a significant negative effect. In contrast, the relationship between substitution practices and use intention is not statistically significant. These findings show that students mainly perceive AI as a tool that supports their learning and academic work, while they are also aware of the risks associated with excessive use. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; higher education; adoption; use intention; students; learning support

items.title: Large Language Models and Augmented Democracy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence enables computational agents to represent political preferences and take part in collective decision-making. In this thesis, I investigate the opportunities and challenges of digital twins (DTs) based on Large Language Models (LLMs) as intermediaries in augmented democracy, focusing on individual preference representation, collective representation of political organizations, and the vulnerability of those representations to attackers. First, using data from an online experiment in Brazil, I examine whether personalized DTs can predict citizens' preferences for unseen policy proposals. Second, I extend the DT framework from individuals to political organizations. Using Swiss parliamentary data, I build topic-specific knowledge graphs from lawmakers' legislative records and connect them to LLM-based lawmaker agents, which are organized into party-level DTs representing collective positions. Agentic deliberation among these agents tests whether aggregated party representations capture a broader range of intra-party perspectives than official party communications. Finally, I study the vulnerability and robustness of LLM-mediated deliberation against prompt-injection attacks that amplify viewpoints, suppress opinions, or redirect consensus. Using data from a 2023 deliberative experiment in the United Kingdom, I analyze how attack effectiveness varies with the distribution of opinions and rhetorical strategies, and evaluate a pipeline combining injection detection, structured opinion representations, and reinforcement learning to improve resistance. These findings characterize the opportunities and challenges of LLM-based digital twins in augmented democracy, stressing accurate preference representation, faithful aggregation, and robustness to strategic interaction.

items.title: Letter of Credit Document Management and Verification: A Review of Traditional, Digital, and Artificial Intelligence-Based Approaches
items.abstract: Letter of Credit (LC) transactions depend on the accurate examination of documentary presentations against the credit terms and applicable documentary-credit rules. Traditionally, this activity has been performed by skilled document checkers, making the process labour-intensive and sensitive to document volume, wording variation, and cross-document inconsistencies. This review examines the evolution of LC document management and verification from manual examination and basic digitisation to intelligent document processing, artificial intelligence, and human-in-the-loop approaches. A structured literature review was conducted using recent peer-reviewed research, international trade rules, and authoritative guidance, with emphasis on developments reported during 2025–2026 while retaining foundational sources required to explain the regulatory and technical context. The literature indicates that optical character recognition, document classification, machine learning, natural language processing, semantic matching, and optimisation can support extraction, consistency checking, discrepancy identification, and workflow prioritisation. Recent research also shifts attention from isolated automation toward hybrid human–AI processes, where AI handles repetitive or high-volume analysis and experienced reviewers handle exceptions and consequential judgments. Digital presentation rules further introduce requirements concerning electronic records, authenticity, integrity, examination, and data corruption. The review identifies persistent gaps in domain-specific datasets, explainability, standardised evaluation, interoperability, governance, and validation under real banking conditions. Future research should therefore focus on auditable, standards-aware, explainable, and human-supervised verification architectures. Keywords— Letter of Credit; Documentary Credit; Document Verification; Intelligent Document Processing; Artificial Intelligence; Human-in-the-Loop

items.title: Lie Rarely, Lie Big: Stealthy Insider Attacks on LLM Robot Teams
items.abstract: When a team of robots delegates planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared outcome. We study this threat in a grounded task: a multi-robot survey in which measurements can be verified against the physical world, but every verification costs budget that would otherwise advance the mission. We treat the compromised robot as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense: it is limited not by an energy bound but by the team's own detectors. We then derive two bounds. First, the probability that the adversary's reports are verified is bounded below in terms of the degrees in the communication graph and the verification budget. Second, the map error caused by any stealthy adversary is bounded above by the value of a linear program over the adversary's bias distributions; its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage: below a critical verification level the worst stealthy attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, and above it the better purchase is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments where the honest robots are LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. The experiments also show that which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.

items.title: Listen to experienced mountaineers… or not? The ‘experience paradox’ of ski tourers’ narratives of risk and experience
items.abstract: Experience is often assumed to reduce risk in ski touring, yet avalanche accidents often involve people perceived to be experienced skiers. Despite increased attention to human factors in avalanche research, little is known about how ski tourers themselves understand and narrate the relationship between experience and risk. Drawing on ten semi-structured in-depth interviews, this article explores ski tourers’ narratives of risk, asking how experience is related to their understanding and description of risk in ski touring. Data were analysed using stepwise deductive-inductive analysis and a sociological framework. The analysis identifies an ‘experience paradox,’ in which experience is portrayed both as a source of safety and as a factor associated with increased risk acceptance and incident involvement. This conceptualization highlights ambiguity in narratives linking experience and risk. The findings also extend research on risk and recognition in lifestyle sports by emphasizing experience as central to distinction and legitimacy in risk-taking.

items.title: LLM-Driven Adaptive Honeypot Framework for Real-Time Cyber Deception and Threat Intelligence
items.abstract: Cyber attackers increasingly use advanced automation and machine learning to detect and evade traditional securitysystems, making static honeypots less effective. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a Generative AI–based honeypot trap design that creates dynamic and realistic decoy environments to better engage and analyze attackers. The aim is to develop a costeffective and scalable solution using AI-generated files, logs, user activity, and system responses to improve deception. The research method includes a comprehensive literature review of honeypots, cyber deception, and generative AI, along with a prototype developed using Python, Flask, and large language models to generate adaptive traps in real time. Early results indicate that generative models can produce highly believable traps that reduce fingerprintability and increase attacker interaction. The system enhances threat monitoring and intelligence by dynamically adjusting to attacker behaviour. Future research will focus on optimizing real-time AI generation, expanding trap diversity, and conducting user testing through penetration simulations.

The aim is to develop a costeffective and scalable solution using AI-generated files, logs, user activity, and system responses to improve deception. The research method includes a comprehensive literature review of honeypots, cyber deception, and generative AI, along with a prototype developed using Python, Flask, and large language models to generate adaptive traps in real time. Early results indicate that generative models can produce highly believable traps that reduce fingerprintability and increase attacker interaction. The system enhances threat monitoring and intelligence by dynamically adjusting to attacker behaviour. Future research will focus on optimizing real-time AI generation, expanding trap diversity, and conducting user testing through penetration simulations.
